newsitem.title: UK: UK again rejects EU role in planned BA-AMR deal.
newsitem.headline: UK again rejects EU role in planned BA-AMR deal.

text.p: Britain restated its objections on Wednesday to a role for the European Commission in judging whether a proposed alliance between British Airways Plc and AMR Corp's American Airlines should go ahead.

"Her Majesty's Government firmly believes that the UK competition authorities possess the necessary powers to investigate and if necessary to approve the proposed alliance," Transport Secretary Sir George Young told parliament.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert repeated his threat on Wednesday to challenge the link-up in the European Court of Justice if Britain approved the deal without taking into account the Brussels-based Commission's worries about competition issues.

Young, speaking in a brief House of Commons debate, said that provided Britain's competition authorities approved the BA-AA alliance, it could provide the basis for a broader deal to liberalise air services between Britain and the United States.
Britain's Office of Fair Trading has provisionally approved the alliance on condition that BA give up 168 weekly take-off and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport.
Long-running negotiations on an "open skies" agreement are due to resume in Washington on February 4.

Young said he could not reveal Britain's negotiating hand but he hoped a deal could be reached that would liberalise transatlantic air traffic to the benefit of customers, British business and airlines.

He rejected a role in the talks for the Commission, which recently obtained a mandate from European Union transport ministers to open exploratory talks with the United States on regulatory issues such as competition rules and airline ownership.

"The mandate, which does not extend to traffic rights, capacity or fares, explicitly states that Member States may continue to negotiate bilaterally, and conclude agreements, with the United States on all matters, including those covered in the mandate," Young's prepared remarks for the debate said.
